```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5)
library(BayesianQDM)
```

This vignette describes the analysis of a proof-of-concept (PoC) study with
one binary endpoint (Kang, Yamaguchi and Han, 2026). `vignette("overview")`
introduces the decision criteria.

## Model

In group $k$ ($k = t$ for treatment, $c$ for control), $y_k$ of $n_k$
subjects respond, $y_k \sim \textrm{Binomial}(n_k, \pi_k)$, and the response
rate has the prior distribution $\pi_k \sim \textrm{Beta}(a_k, b_k)$
(`prior_beta()`; `prior_beta(0.5, 0.5)` is the Jeffreys prior). The
posterior distribution is
$$\pi_k \mid y_k \sim \textrm{Beta}(a_k + y_k, b_k + n_k - y_k),$$
and the treatment effect is $\theta = \pi_t - \pi_c$. The posterior
probability $\Pr(\theta > q \mid D)$ is computed by numerical integration
(`pbetadiff()`).

For the predictive criterion, $m_k$ future subjects of group $k$ have
$\tilde y_k$ responders, whose posterior predictive distribution is
beta-binomial. The future effect is
$\tilde\theta = \tilde y_t / m_t - \tilde y_c / m_c$, and its predictive
probabilities are computed exactly by summation (`pbetabinomdiff()`).

## Decision for observed data

A study with 12 subjects in each group, Jeffreys priors and a posterior
criterion with $\theta_{TV} = 0.2$, $\theta_{MAV} = 0.1$,
$\gamma_{go} = 0.5$ and $\gamma_{nogo} = 0.8$:

```{r design}
jeffreys <- prior_beta(0.5, 0.5)
crit <- criterion_posterior(theta_tv = 0.2, theta_mav = 0.1,
                            gamma_go = 0.5, gamma_nogo = 0.8)
des <- design_binary(n_t = 12, n_c = 12, prior_t = jeffreys,
                     prior_c = jeffreys, criterion = crit)
dec <- qdm_decide(des, data_t = data_binary(12, 9),
                  data_c = data_binary(12, 3))
dec
```

The probabilities of the Go and NoGo regions are the posterior probabilities
$\Pr(\theta > 0.2 \mid D)$ and $\Pr(\theta \le 0.1 \mid D)$, which
`pbetadiff()` gives from the posterior parameters:

```{r pbetadiff}
post_t <- dec$posterior_t
post_c <- dec$posterior_c
pbetadiff(0.2, a_t = post_t[["a"]], b_t = post_t[["b"]],
          a_c = post_c[["a"]], b_c = post_c[["b"]], lower.tail = FALSE)
pbetadiff(0.1, a_t = post_t[["a"]], b_t = post_t[["b"]],
          a_c = post_c[["a"]], b_c = post_c[["b"]])
```

With 9 and 3 responders, the decision is `r dec$decision`.

## Forms of the control group

### External control data

External data enter through a power prior: with $n_e$ subjects,
$y_e$ responders and weight $a_0$ (from 0 to 1), the posterior distribution
of the response rate is
$$\textrm{Beta}(a + a_0 y_e + y, \; b + a_0 (n_e - y_e) + n - y).$$
With $a_0 = 0$ the external data are ignored, and with $a_0 = 1$ they are
pooled with the current data. Borrowing half of 20 external control
subjects with 5 responders:

```{r external}
des_ext <- design_binary(
  n_t = 12, n_c = 12, prior_t = jeffreys, prior_c = jeffreys,
  criterion = crit,
  external_c = borrow(data_binary(n = 20, y = 5), a0 = 0.5)
)
dec_ext <- qdm_decide(des_ext, data_t = data_binary(12, 9),
                      data_c = data_binary(12, 3))
dec_ext$posterior_c
```

The external data add
`r dec_ext$posterior_c[["a"]] - dec$posterior_c[["a"]]` responders and
`r dec_ext$posterior_c[["b"]] - dec$posterior_c[["b"]]` non-responders to the
posterior distribution of the control group, and the
probability of the Go region becomes
`r format(dec_ext$prob_go, digits = 3)` (without them,
`r format(dec$prob_go, digits = 3)`).

Without a concurrent control group (`n_c = 0`), the control group can be
described by the external data alone:

```{r external-only}
des_ext0 <- design_binary(
  n_t = 12, n_c = 0, prior_t = jeffreys, prior_c = jeffreys,
  criterion = crit,
  external_c = borrow(data_binary(n = 40, y = 10), a0 = 1)
)
qdm_decide(des_ext0, data_t = data_binary(12, 9))
```

External treatment data (`external_t`) can be used in the same way with any
form of the control group.

### Hypothetical control

For an uncontrolled study, Kang et al. (2026, Section 4.1.4) describe the
control response rate by a hypothetical control,
$\pi_c \sim \textrm{Beta}(a_t + z, b_t + n_t - z)$, where $z$ is the number
of responders expected among $n_t$ control subjects. This is obtained with
`prior_c` equal to `prior_t` and `hypothetical(data_binary(n_t, z))`:

```{r hypothetical}
des_hyp <- design_binary(
  n_t = 12, n_c = 0, prior_t = jeffreys, prior_c = jeffreys,
  criterion = crit,
  hypothetical_c = hypothetical(data = data_binary(n = 12, y = 3))
)
qdm_decide(des_hyp, data_t = data_binary(12, 9))
```

### Fixed control

A single-arm study is often compared with a known benchmark, such as the
response rate of the standard of care reported in the literature. With
`fixed_c`, the control response rate is a known value $\pi_{c0}$, the
treatment effect is $\theta = \pi_t - \pi_{c0}$, and `prior_c` is not used
(it must be `NULL`). The probability of the Go region is then the Beta
probability $\Pr(\pi_t > \pi_{c0} + \theta_{TV} \mid D)$. A study with 20
subjects compared with a benchmark of 0.2:

```{r fixed}
crit_fix <- criterion_posterior(theta_tv = 0.2, theta_mav = 0.05,
                                gamma_go = 0.8, gamma_nogo = 0.8)
des_fix <- design_binary(n_t = 20, n_c = 0, prior_t = prior_beta(1, 1),
                         criterion = crit_fix, fixed_c = 0.2)
dec_fix <- qdm_decide(des_fix, data_t = data_binary(20, 11))
dec_fix
pbeta(0.2 + 0.2, 1 + 11, 1 + 20 - 11, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

With `fixed_c = 0`, the effect is the response rate itself, and the
thresholds are response rates. For the predictive criterion, the future
effect is $\tilde y_t / m_t - \pi_{c0}$, and `m_c` is not used.

## Predictive criterion

The predictive criterion asks whether a future study with $m_t$ and $m_c$
subjects would observe an effect larger than $\theta_{NULL}$. With 40
subjects per group in the future study and $\theta_{NULL} = 0$:

```{r predictive}
des_pred <- design_binary(
  n_t = 12, n_c = 12, prior_t = jeffreys, prior_c = jeffreys,
  criterion = criterion_predictive(theta_null = 0, m_t = 40,
                                   gamma_go = 0.9, gamma_nogo = 0.7)
)
dec_pred <- qdm_decide(des_pred, data_t = data_binary(12, 9),
                       data_c = data_binary(12, 3))
dec_pred
post_t <- dec_pred$posterior_t
post_c <- dec_pred$posterior_c
pbetabinomdiff(0, m_t = 40, a_t = post_t[["a"]], b_t = post_t[["b"]],
               m_c = 40, a_c = post_c[["a"]], b_c = post_c[["b"]],
               lower.tail = FALSE)
```

The Go and NoGo regions of the predictive criterion are complementary, so
their probabilities add up to 1. A Gray decision is then possible only when
$\gamma_{go} + \gamma_{nogo} > 1$.

## Operating characteristics

`qdm_oc()` computes the probabilities of Go, NoGo, Gray and Miss decisions
under scenarios for the true response rates. All outcomes
$(y_t, y_c)$ of the study are enumerated and weighted by their binomial
probabilities, so the results are exact.

```{r oc}
oc <- qdm_oc(des, data.frame(pi_t = seq(0.2, 0.8, by = 0.05), pi_c = 0.2))
oc
plot(oc)
```

The vertical lines mark the effects $\theta_{MAV}$ and $\theta_{TV}$. For
the uncontrolled design, the horizontal axis is the response rate of the
treatment group, and the lines are shifted by the mean of the hypothetical
control distribution:

```{r oc-hyp}
oc_hyp <- qdm_oc(des_hyp, data.frame(pi_t = seq(0.2, 0.8, by = 0.05)))
plot(oc_hyp)
```

## Decision boundary

`qdm_boundary()` gives the decision for every possible outcome of the study,
and its plot shows which outcomes lead to Go, NoGo and Gray decisions.
Unlike the operating characteristics, it does not depend on the true
response rates. For the design with a concurrent control group, the axes are
the numbers of responders of the two groups:

```{r boundary}
plot(qdm_boundary(des))
```

Without a concurrent control group, the boundary is shown for several sample
sizes of the treatment group, here from 10 to 40 subjects for the design
with a fixed control:

```{r boundary-fixed}
b_fix <- qdm_boundary(des_fix, n_t = 10:40)
plot(b_fix)
```

With 20 subjects, a Go decision needs at least
`r min(b_fix$y_t[b_fix$n_t == 20 & b_fix$decision == "Go"])` responders, and
the decision is NoGo with at most
`r max(b_fix$y_t[b_fix$n_t == 20 & b_fix$decision == "NoGo"])` responders.

## Calibration of the thresholds

`qdm_calibrate()` chooses $\gamma_{go}$ as the smallest value of a grid for
which the probability of meeting the Go criterion under `scenario_go` is at
most `target_go`, and $\gamma_{nogo}$ in the same way for the NoGo criterion
under `scenario_nogo`. Here the Go criterion should be met with probability
at most 0.05 when the treatment has no effect, and the NoGo criterion with
probability at most 0.2 when the effect is 0.3:

```{r calibrate}
cal <- qdm_calibrate(des,
                     scenario_go = data.frame(pi_t = 0.2, pi_c = 0.2),
                     scenario_nogo = data.frame(pi_t = 0.5, pi_c = 0.2),
                     target_go = 0.05, target_nogo = 0.2)
cal
plot(cal)
```

The chosen thresholds are $\gamma_{go} =$ `r cal$gamma_go` and
$\gamma_{nogo} =$ `r cal$gamma_nogo`. The design with these thresholds is
`cal$design`:

```{r calibrated-oc}
qdm_oc(cal$design, data.frame(pi_t = c(0.2, 0.35, 0.5), pi_c = 0.2))
```

## Reference

Kang, R., Yamaguchi, Y. and Han, C. (2026). Bayesian quantitative
decision-making framework in cell and gene therapy development for rare
diseases. *Journal of Biopharmaceutical Statistics*.
<https://doi.org/10.1080/10543406.2026.2655410>
